title: Psalm 121: The LORD Who Keeps You
summary: A traveler looks up at the hills and asks where help will come from, then answers: from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth. A second voice takes up the answer and turns it into a blessing, promising that the LORD who never sleeps will keep the traveler from stumbling, from the sun by day and the moon by night, and from all evil, on every road out and every road home.
story: Psalm 121 is the second of the fifteen Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120 to 134), a small collection inside Book V of the Psalter. Psalm 120 began far from Jerusalem, with a speaker living among people who hate peace; Psalm 121 puts that speaker on the road, with the hills ahead, and Psalm 122 will bring him through the gates of the city. Read in order, the collection moves from exile toward the house of the LORD, and this psalm is the moment of setting out. Its question, where help comes from, is the question every pilgrim asks at the start of the road, and its answer carries through the rest of the collection: Psalm 124 ends with nearly the same words, calling the LORD the Maker of heaven and earth.
historical:
The heading reads simply “A song of ascents”, with no author named. The Hebrew phrase, shir hamma'alot, means a song of the goings up or of the steps, and scholars have read it in several ways. The most common view connects the collection with the pilgrim festivals: Israel's law called every man to appear before the LORD three times a year, at Passover (with the Feast of Unleavened Bread), at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:16), and people spoke of going up to Jerusalem because it sits high in the hill country of Judah. A second view, preserved in the Mishnah (the early rabbinic collection of Jewish law, compiled around AD 200), says the Levites sang on the fifteen steps that led up between courts of the temple, one song for each step. A third reads the heading in light of the return from Babylon, which Ezra 7:9 calls a going up. Others think it describes the poetry itself, which climbs by repeating a word from one line in the next.

The psalm cannot be dated with confidence. Most scholars place the collection in its present form after the exile, in the Persian period (539 to 332 BC), when Jews from scattered places came up to a rebuilt temple, though many of its songs may be older. Nothing in Psalm 121 ties it to a single event. It fits any pilgrim, in any century, who faced the hills between home and Jerusalem.
cultural:
Travel in ancient Israel was on foot, over rough limestone paths, through country where a turned ankle could be serious and where bandits used the hills for cover (the parable of the Good Samaritan assumes the road down to Jericho was dangerous). The hills in verse 1 can be read two ways. They may be the hills around Jerusalem, the goal of the trip, toward which the pilgrim looks with longing. Or they may be the threatening heights along the way, where the shrines of other gods often stood on hilltops, so that the question means: will help come from the gods of the high places? Either way, the answer points past the hills to the one who made them.

The dangers named in verse 6 are real ones. Sunstroke was a known killer in a hot, dry land (many readers take the boy in 2 Kings 4:18-20, who cried out about his head in the harvest field and died, as a case of it). Many ancient peoples also believed the moon could harm a person, bringing fever or madness; the Greek word behind the epileptic boy in Matthew 17:15 literally means moonstruck. The psalm answers both fears. The promise that Israel's Protector never sleeps also carried an edge in that world, where other gods were imagined as sleeping, traveling, or distracted; Elijah mocked the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel by suggesting their god might be asleep (1 Kings 18:27).
literary: The psalm is built on one word. The Hebrew verb shamar, to keep or guard, appears six times in eight verses, translated by the BSB as “your Protector”, “the Protector of Israel”, “your keeper”, “will guard”, “will preserve”, and “will watch over”. The first two verses are spoken in the first person (“My help comes from the LORD”), and from verse 3 on someone addresses the traveler as you, which suggests a dialogue: a pilgrim's confession answered by the blessing of a companion, a family member, or a priest. The poem also shows the stair-step pattern that marks the Songs of Ascents, where a word from one line is picked up and carried higher in the next: help in verses 1 and 2, slumber in verses 3 and 4, keeper and keep through verses 5 to 8. The closing line widens to its largest frame, “your coming and going, both now and forevermore”, a Hebrew way of saying all of life, every departure and every return.

outline.t: The pilgrim's question and confession: help from the Maker
Shade by day and by night
Kept from all evil, going and coming, forever

doctrines.note: God's care reaches down to the traveler's foot on a loose stone and the heat of a single afternoon. The psalm does not promise that nothing hard will happen; it promises that the one who keeps Israel is awake and attending at every moment.

The answer to the pilgrim's question rests on who God is: “the Maker of heaven and earth”. The one who made the hills, the sun, and the moon is not threatened by any of them, so the creator is the only fitting source of help.
Unlike the sleeping gods of the nations, the LORD “will neither slumber nor sleep.” His attention does not lapse, and his keeping of one traveler is of a piece with his keeping of all Israel.

words.note: Shamar, to keep, guard, watch over. It is the verb for a watchman on a wall, a shepherd with a flock, and the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24, where the LORD blesses and keeps his people. Its six uses here make the psalm one extended description of God as keeper, moving from the feet (verse 3) to the soul (verse 7) to the whole of a life (verse 8).

Ezer, help or helper. It is used most often of God's help to people who cannot help themselves, and it is the same word used for the woman in Genesis 2:18, where it carries no sense of inferiority. The pilgrim asks where ezer comes from and answers that it comes from the LORD, not from the hills or anything on them.

Tsel, shade or shadow. In a land of hard sun, shade meant life and relief, and a king's shadow was a picture of his protection. To call the LORD “the shade on your right hand” pictures him standing at the traveler's side, close enough to cover him, the right hand being the side of strength and of a defender.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 121, so its link to Christ is thematic rather than predictive, but the theme runs deep. Jesus speaks of himself as the good shepherd from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28), and in his prayer the night before his death he tells the Father that he kept and guarded the disciples while he was with them and asks the Father to keep them still (John 17:11-12). Jude ends his letter by praising the God who is able to keep believers from stumbling (Jude 24), an echo of the foot that will not slip. There is also a striking contrast in the Gospels: the God who never sleeps became a man who fell asleep in a boat in a storm (Mark 4:38), and the disciples found that even then they were not unguarded.

hard.q: Does this psalm promise that nothing bad will ever happen to those who trust God?
hard.a: Read quickly, verse 7 (“The LORD will guard you from all evil”) could sound like a guarantee against every harm. But the people who sang it knew otherwise: pilgrims were robbed, fell ill, and died, and the Psalter itself is full of laments from faithful people who suffered. Some interpreters take “evil” here as moral evil or final ruin rather than every hardship, so that the promise is that nothing can destroy the life God keeps. Others read the psalm as a blessing spoken over a traveler, a statement of God's character and ordinary care, rather than a contract that rules out suffering. Both readings note that verse 7 says “He will preserve your soul”, and the Hebrew nephesh means the whole living self; the New Testament extends that keeping beyond death. The psalm offers confidence in a keeper, not immunity from the road.

questions: Where do you instinctively look for help first, before you look to God? What are your hills?
The psalm moves from a first-person confession to a blessing spoken by someone else. Who has spoken God's keeping over you when you could not say it yourself, and for whom could you do the same?
What would change in how you face the coming and going of an ordinary week if you believed the one keeping you never sleeps?
